lines.text: Data Engineering opens with five short refreshers. They are not lessons, they are checks.
This first one is Python: the parts a senior engineer relies on when reviewing someone else's code, and the language our pipelines are written in.
If every slide feels familiar, good. Swipe on to Git. If one surprises you, that is the one worth ten minutes.
Start with a trap that catches experienced people. A function has a default argument, an empty list.
Ask yourself when that list is made. Not when you call the function, but when the definition runs, once.
So what does the second call return?
Both calls share one list, so the second call returns the first call's item as well.
A function is an object, and its defaults are stored on it. Every call that omits the argument gets the same list.
The usual fix is to default to nothing, and build the list inside the function. The other three answers all assume a fresh list per call.
Its cousin lives in loops. Three small functions are created inside a loop, each returning the loop variable.
Think about when a function looks a name up. When it is created, or when it runs?
What do the three return?
The last value, three times.
Each function looks the name up when it runs, and by then the loop has finished, so the variable holds its final value.
To capture the value now, give it as a default argument, which is evaluated at definition time, the same fact as the last slide, used on purpose.
A comprehension is a filter and a map written as one expression. Read it left to right: what to produce, then where from, then the test.
The same shape builds dictionaries and sets, not just lists.
One small detail worth remembering: the loop variable stays inside the comprehension and does not leak into the surrounding code.
Now memory, which is where Python stops being only a convenience. Look at the two lines on screen.
They compute the same sum. The first builds a list of a million numbers before it adds anything. The second hands them over one at a time.
The difference is tens of megabytes against half a kilobyte, and it grows with the input.
That is how a pipeline can read a file larger than its memory. It never holds the file.
How does a function hand over one value at a time? With the keyword that makes it a generator.
Follow the pointer in the code. Each request runs the body up to the next yield, returns that value, and freezes right there with all its local state.
The next request wakes it exactly where it stopped.
That is enough to batch a stream in a handful of lines, with nothing held in between.
Resources need a guarantee: whatever happens, release them. A file, a connection, a lock, a transaction.
The with block gives it. When the block ends, normally or by an error, the cleanup code runs.
Writing your own is short with a decorator: setup before the yield, and teardown after it, inside a finally so that an error cannot skip it.
The finally is the part people forget, and it is the whole point.

lines.text: A decorator is a function that takes a function and returns a replacement. Placing it above a definition is only shorthand for that reassignment.
Retrying, caching, timing and permission checks are almost always written this way, because they wrap behaviour around code without touching it.
One thing to remember: copy the original's name and documentation across with the standard helper. Otherwise every log line says wrapper, and nobody can tell which function ran.

lines.text: Classes carry a lot of boilerplate, and a dataclass writes it for you: the constructor, a readable printout, and equality.
Two options matter in data work. Frozen makes instances immutable, which makes them safe to share.
Slots removes the per object dictionary. With millions of small records, that is a real memory saving, not a micro optimisation.

lines.text: Special methods are how a class plugs into the language. One lets a loop walk through it, one gives it a length, one defines what equal means.
Here is the catch. The moment you define equality, Python quietly removes the hash. A dataclass defines equality for you.
A dictionary key has to be hashable, and equal objects must hash equally, otherwise lookups break.
So, can this record serve as a dictionary key?
No, you get an error saying the type is unhashable.
A record that can change after it is stored could silently break the dictionary, so Python refuses to hash it.
Freeze it and it works. Frozen means it cannot change, so equal objects keep hashing equally.
Last trap. A function says its argument is a whole number.
Think about who enforces that statement while the program runs.
Now pass it a string.
What happens?
It just works, and returns the string repeated. Nothing at runtime checks the hint.
Hints are for tools. A type checker reads them and finds this before it ships.
So the hint only protects you if something is checking it. Run a checker in CI, or treat the hint as a comment.
Nine things to keep, in a sentence each.
Defaults run once. Closures look names up late. Comprehensions filter, then map. Generators stream, lists pile up.
A with block always cleans up. Decorators wrap. Dataclasses write the boilerplate. Equal objects need equal hashes. Hints are checked by tools, not by Python.
Anything rusty? The prerequisites panel points to good places to refresh it. Otherwise, on to Git.
